catalog_quote: 3. Prosodic phonemes are stress /´/ and length /·/. Stress and length may occur on any vowel and any position in the word. Length does not alter the quality of the vowel with which it occurs; the lengthening-effect is slight. Its phonemic status is attested by the following word pairs: pulʼáypa he carried in arms, pu·lʼáypa it suppurated; xakʼepá he got lost, xa·kʼepá he agreed. Stress is associated with the vowel rather than with the syllable. Its phonemic status is attested by the following word pairs: sánna small crawfish, sanná star; fáneʔ three, fanéʔ well-worn. There appear to be certain types of shift of stress with certain intonation patterns. Intonational lengthening for emphasis also occurs. new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is a phoneme in its own right: it is not fixed to any position, may fall on any vowel in any position of the word, and distinguishes minimal pairs (sánna vs sanná, fáneʔ vs fanéʔ); i.e. lexically contrastive, unpredictable stress. Stress may shift under certain intonation contours.
new_statements.exceptions: Only that 'certain types of shift of stress' occur with certain intonation patterns; no positional default or exceptions stated. (Maddieson et al. 2005 add that monosyllabic stems 'seem to have a higher level of stress' and note pretonic vowel lengthening, but give no placement rule.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonemic stress in citation forms; interaction with phrase intonation noted (final syllable of statements high, etc.). The 1950 paper names the language only as 'Chontal (Tequistlateco)' of southern Oaxaca; Waterhouse's companion 1949 paper on the same 1942-48 field data states it concerns 'only the dialect spoken on the coast' (Huamelula), i.e. Lowland/Huamelultec = lowl1260.
new_statements.identity_note: Waterhouse & Morrison 1950 call the language simply 'Chontal (also called Tequistlateco)' of southern Oaxaca with 8000-9000 speakers (a figure covering both Highland and Lowland). The data are from Waterhouse's 1942-48 SIL fieldwork; her companion paper on the same data (IJAL 15:106, 1949) says it is 'concerned only with the dialect spoken on the coast; I have no data on the Sierra dialect', and her 1967 HMAI sketch (snippet) says 'The present description is only of Huamelultec.. spoken in the villages of Astata and Huamelula'. So the described variety is Lowland/Huamelultec Chontal = lowl1260, not Highland Chontal (high1242, Turner's 'Tequistlatec'). Maddieson et al. 2005 recorded speakers in San Pedro Huamelula (same variety).

readall_conflicts: No disagreement about stress among the sources read. The only clash is about vowel length, not stress: Waterhouse & Morrison 1950 (catalog quote) treat length /·/ as a second prosodic phoneme beside stress, whereas Maddieson, Avelino & O'Connor (2005/2009, p. 233) found no contrastive length in six speakers and describe lengthening as allophonic and 'frequently in pretonic syllables'. Waterhouse 1967 could not be opened (lending-only archive.org item, 401/403 on every route); second-hand snippets (Maddieson et al. citing her /amác'/ 'year', and the Google Books snippet of her 1962 grammar on penultimate-stressed nouns shifting stress to the final syllable in the plural) are compatible with, not contrary to, the catalog's lexical-stress reading.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No rule for stress placement. States the phonology 'involves neither tone nor phonation contrasts on syllable nuclei'; vowels show allophonic lengthening 'frequently in pretonic syllables'; formants measured 'in stressed syllables'; transcriptions carry IPA stress marks (e.g. /akaˈn'oʔ/ 'woman', /akaɬˈnoʔ/ 'women', final-syllable stress) and monosyllabic stems 'seem to have a higher level of stress'. Confirms a stress language but is silent on where stress falls.
